activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman described the availability heuristic in 1973: people judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
story:
At dinner Hayden pushed his noodles around the plate and said he wasn't going on the beach trip Saturday. His dad looked up from his glass. "Since when? You've been talking about it for a month."

"Braxton's uncle got bitten by a shark last summer," Hayden said. "Right off that same beach. Braxton told me at lunch. He said the water turned red and the uncle needed forty stitches and now he won't even take a bath." The image was so clear that Hayden could perceive the whole scene, the fin, the splashing, people screaming on the sand, even though he had never been there.

"That's one guy," his sister said, reaching for the bread.

"One guy is enough," Hayden said. His mom mentioned that his grandfather had been in a car accident once and still drove every day, but Hayden said that was different. It didn't feel different to anyone else at the table, but nobody could convince him between the salad and the main course, so the conversation drifted to his cousin's new job at a company that had been around forever, practically a dynasty in the towel business, and then back to whether Hayden was being gullible, believing Braxton's story without checking anything.

Hayden pulled out his phone, which he was allowed to do for homework reasons only, and typed a message to Frederique: name every shark attack you've ever heard of. Then: name every drowning you've ever heard of. Frederique wrote back two shark stories and zero drownings. Then Hayden found the actual numbers for that beach, and the drownings were higher than the shark bites, several times higher, every single year he checked. He sat there with the phone under the table, holding two facts that pointed opposite directions.

"It's called the availability heuristic," Frederique texted a minute later. "Tversky and Kahneman, 1973. People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind." Hayden read it twice. Braxton's uncle's blood in the water came to mind instantly, red and sharp. The drownings came to mind as nothing at all, just numbers on a screen, which was exactly the problem.

He set the phone face down and picked up his fork. "I'm going Saturday," he said.

"Because you did the math or because your noodles got cold?" his dad asked.

"Because one story is loud and a hundred quiet ones aren't." He ate a noodle, then another, and slid his plate toward his mom for seconds.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: When defenders switch on a pick and roll, it can create a mismatch, such as a tall player guarding a quick guard or a short player guarding a tall one.
story:
Evelyn stood at the top of the key on the cracked concrete pad behind the hockey rink, where the summer league practiced when the ice was out. The zamboni driver had left the gate open, and the smell of cold rubber drifted out every time the door swung. Kassidy waved for the ball from the wing, and Cael set up at the elbow, waiting.

"Run it," Kassidy called. The play was a pick and roll. Cael was supposed to sprint over and plant himself beside Evelyn's defender, and Evelyn would dribble off his shoulder toward the basket. They had run it six times in practice, and six times the coach had blown the whistle because Evelyn passed too early or too late. Now it was scrimmage, and the coach was watching from a folding chair near the boards.

Evelyn signaled with two raised fingers, and Cael came hard. She dragged her dribble off the pick. Behind her, the two defenders did something she had not expected: they switched. Cael's defender slid over to guard Evelyn, and Cael's own man, the smallest player on the other team, a kid named only as number eleven, ended up stuck against Cael, who was eight inches taller.

Evelyn pulled her dribble back out and held up a hand. She thought it through the way she thought through her science worksheet, the one still folded in her pocket next to her notes about how a larva turns into a beetle. The defenders had made a choice, and that choice had left a small kid guarding a tall kid. She could not see the rule written anywhere, but she could test it. "Cael, post up," she said, and fired the ball over the switching defender's head. Cael caught it, turned, and laid it in over number eleven's outstretched arms.

"That's twice," Kassidy said, jogging back on defense. "They keep switching."

"Then we keep going to Cael," Evelyn said. The next time down, they ran the same play. The defenders switched again, and again the smallest one ended up on Cael. Evelyn coordinated it without shouting, just a small nod at Cael and a bounce pass in before the other team could react. Cael scored again. On the third trip, the defenders panicked. They barked at each other and half-switched, half-stayed, which was worse than either one. Evelyn drove through the gap and scored herself.

After the scrimmage, Mr. Santoso, who ran the summer league and lived two streets from the rink, picked up the ball and spun it on one finger. "That last one was a little reckless," he said to Evelyn.

"It worked," Evelyn said.

He handed her the ball. "Run it once more. Both of you, full speed."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when proteins in wheat flour mix with water, and kneading the dough makes the gluten stronger and stretchier.
story:
The farmers' market smelled like kettle corn and wet lettuce, and Eli walked past all of it heading straight for the stone-ground flour stall. Ms. Kaminski ran it, and she saved him the last paper sack of hard red wheat flour every Saturday because she knew what his Saturdays revolved around now: baking bread for his family while his mother worked the double shift.

"You look worried," she said, weighing the sack.

"The last loaf was a brick," Eli said. "I did everything Grandpa wrote on the card. Flour, water, salt, yeast, let it rise." He had kneaded it, too, but only until it looked smooth, maybe three minutes, because his arms got tired and the recipe card just said knead until smooth.

Yann, who had tagged along for the free samples, was skeptical. "Maybe your oven's broken. Ovens break."

"Or you bought bad flour," said Micaela, who was skeptical of almost nothing except flour.

Eli stood there turning the problem over. His mother had said the crumb was dense and tight, like a doorstop. On television he had once watched a baker stretch a piece of pale dough until it went thin as a windowpane without tearing, and the baker had held it up and said one word: gluten. He hadn't thought about it again until now. If the dough needed to be stretchy and his wasn't, maybe the stretchiness was the hidden thing. Maybe it didn't exist in the flour at all until water touched it, and maybe it took real time to build.

At home, he set out two bowls and ran an experiment. In the first, he mixed flour and water and kneaded for ten full minutes by the clock, resting when his wrists ached, while his little sister sat on the counter and counted out loud to keep him honest. In the second, he kneaded for three minutes. He pulled a walnut of dough from each and stretched them side by side. The short one tore right away. The long one stretched and stretched, thin enough to see his sister's fingers through it, before it finally gave.

Grandpa called that evening, and Eli held the phone close. "I figured out the brick," he said. "Ten minutes of kneading. Not until it looks smooth. Ten minutes, and the dough turns into a network that holds the bubbles when it rises." Grandpa laughed so hard Eli had to hold the phone away from his ear.

The new loaf came out of the oven golden and tall, and when Eli tore it open, the inside was full of holes, big and small, like a sponge. His mother got home at nine, cold and tired, and he met her at the door with the bread still warm and a dish of butter. "Try it," he said, and held out the knife.

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
Joshua had until Friday to figure out what to do about Quinten, and Friday was two days away. Quinten had been teased at lunch all week, mostly about the stutter that showed up when he got excited, and Joshua had just sat there gripping his fork. At home that evening he flopped onto the couch with his mom's laptop and typed "how to help someone being teased." Most of what came up was useless, but one page stopped him cold. A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes. He read it twice. Almost nine times out of ten, somebody else was watching too.

He scrolled further and found a message board where a kid had posted the same question he had. "I want to enroll in this school's anti-bullying program," one reply began, "but honestly what changed things wasn't the program." Joshua leaned closer to the screen. The reply went on: "When the teasing started, a girl next to me just said something normal to the kid being teased, like the teasers weren't even there. She talked to him about homework. It broke it up without a fight." Joshua copied the reply and texted it to Melanie, who had also been sitting at that lunch table doing nothing.

Melanie called him back within minutes. "So you noticed too," she said. "I keep thinking somebody should say something, but if you yell at them, they just come after you, and then it's worse for Quinten because he feels like a little kid being rescued."

"That's what I keep getting stuck on," Joshua said. "But here's the thing I found. That 2001 playground study, other kids were there during 88 percent of bullying episodes. Which means everybody at that table is watching. Including the two kids who do the teasing. They know they have an audience."

"So the audience is the problem," Melanie said slowly. "Or it could be the solution."

They agreed to test it at lunch on Friday, which happened to be the day the counselor came around with flyers about the exceptional students nominated for the district scholarship. Joshua got to the cafeteria early and claimed the seat next to Quinten. When the two boys started in, mimicking the way Quinten's words snagged, Joshua didn't look at them at all. He turned to Quinten and asked, loud enough for the whole table, whether he'd finished the science questions. Melanie leaned in on the other side and asked about problem six.

Quinten took a breath, and his answer came out slow but steady, because he was talking about something he actually cared about. The mimicking stuttered and stopped. One of the teasers glanced around the table, found no audience paying attention, and went back to his pizza.

After school, Joshua found a folded note in his backpack, in Quinten's careful handwriting. "Thanks for asking me about the science," it read. "Question six took me forever. Want to compare answers Monday?"

Joshua grinned and texted Melanie a photo of the note. "Monday," she wrote back.

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Emmett had built his reading nook out of two couch cushions, a beach umbrella, and a flashlight taped to a broom handle, and he was proud of every component of it. He crawled inside with his copy of "The Scarlet Ibis" and a letter Mr. Katz had handed back that afternoon. The letter was from Zorawar, who had moved away in October and still wrote actual letters because his new town had terrible wifi.

"Dear Emmett," Zorawar had written. "I finished the story before you did, so ha. When the red bird gets blown into the garden by the storm and dies, I had a weird feeling about it. Then I read the part about Doodle and I actually said 'oh no' out loud on the bus. Also I bet five jelly beans you don't figure out why the author did that. Your friend, Zorawar. P.S. Five jelly beans is a lot, so think hard."

Emmett read the story again, slower this time. A storm-blown red bird, a scarlet ibis, far from where it belonged, dies in the family's garden. It seemed like just a sad thing that happens. But then he noticed that Doodle, the fragile boy who was always being pushed to do more than his body could manage, kept showing up in the same colors, the same exhausted way. He flipped back and forth between the pages so many times the flashlight wobbled.

He grabbed his phone and typed a message to Christina, who was still awake because she claimed she was "studying," which meant reading about sharks. "The bird is a setup," he wrote. "Like when a movie shows the canoe early. It's telling you what's going to happen to Doodle. It stands for him too. Zorawar owes me jelly beans." Christina replied with a single shark emoji, then, a minute later, "Wait. Say more. I want to use this on Monday and look smart in front of Mr. Katz." That was Christina's whole plan for the week, and Emmett knew it, so he sent her one more line about how the storm that blew the bird in matched the storm at the end.

The next morning Emmett found Zorawar's replacement at the desk beside his, a kid who chewed pencils like a defiant beaver, and lent him a pencil just to be friendly. In English, Mr. Katz asked what the ibis might be doing in the story, and Christina raised her hand so fast her chair screeched. She gave almost the whole idea, clearly, and even said the word foreshadowing out loud, and Mr. Katz said, "Excellent." Emmett leaned over after class and tried to confide in her that half that answer was his.

"Half?" Christina said. "I added the part about the color red. That's the whole other component." She was already unwrapping a bag of jelly beans, though, and she counted out five and set them on his desk without looking at him. "From Zorawar's stash," she said. "He mailed them to me for safekeeping. Don't tell him I lost."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: The protagonist is a story's main character, and the antagonist is the character or force working against them; their conflict drives the plot toward the climax.
story:
Mackenzie stared at the third draft of her story and counted the quotation marks. There were nine. That seemed like too many for a story about a girl lost in a blizzard, but she wasn't sure, because nobody had ever taught her how to incorporate dialogue into a paragraph without the whole thing collapsing into comma soup.

"You moved a comma again," said Samar, sliding into the chair across from her. He had a library pass that said research, and his research so far appeared to be watching her suffer.

"The comma goes inside the quotation marks," Henri said from the next table, not looking up. "I learned that the hard way. Mr. Asante circled mine in red pen. Twice. On the same sentence."

Mackenzie looked at her page. "But it looks wrong in there. It looks trapped."

"Trapped is fine," Henri said. "Trapped is correct."

She fixed the comma and then read the story aloud in a whisper, which was the only volume the library permitted. The girl in the story, Pru, had to get home before the roads closed. Halfway through, a man at a gas station refused to sell her a map, and Mackenzie had written three whole pages about their argument.

Samar frowned. "Why is she still arguing with that guy? The storm's getting worse. I keep waiting for the storm."

"The guy is the antagonist," Mackenzie said. "He's against her. He's the whole problem."

"Is he, though?" Samar turned her page back. "The snow started before he showed up. He's just one guy with a bad attitude. The snow is everywhere."

Mackenzie sat with that. In her head she lined up the story's pieces like evidence. The storm closed the road. The storm cut the power. The storm was the thing making every choice urgent. The man with the map was annoying, but he wasn't the force working against Pru. The conflict that pushed the story forward, all the way to its biggest moment, was snow.

"So the antagonist doesn't have to be a person," she said slowly. "It can be a force. And the protagonist is just whoever the story's about, the one the antagonist is working against. Their fight is what drives everything toward the climax."

"Sure," said Samar, who had clearly never doubted it.

She crossed out three pages. It hurt a little. On the new page, Pru stopped arguing with the map man, walked out into the white, and had to decide whether to shelter in the empty school or push the last mile home. That was the climax Mackenzie had been missing, and it had been sitting there in the weather the whole time.

Mr. Asante passed by on his way to the circulation desk and paused. "Is that the dialogue assignment? Finished?"

"Almost," Mackenzie said. "Turns out my antagonist was never in the gas station. It was falling out of the sky the entire time."

Mr. Asante considered this, then glanced out the window, where fat flakes had started coming down over the parking lot.

"You might want to check the bus schedule," he said.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
story:
The community hall smelled like onions and warm bread, and Paisley's stomach growled so loudly that Ely heard it over the noise of two hundred people. "Save it," Paisley told her stomach, which did not listen. Her family had come straight from her little brother's soccer game, and there was no time for snacks, because her mother had promised they would help before the hall filled up. The deadline was real: the volunteers needed the roti baskets refilled before the doors opened at noon, and it was already five minutes to.

Damian trailed behind them, clutching his phone. He had a plan for the day, which was to film an "eloquent documentary" about the celebration for his social studies teacher, and he kept practicing dramatic narration under his breath. "As the crowd gathers, hungry and unaware of what awaits them," he murmured, until Ely elbowed him. "You sound like a nature show," she said. Ely's own plan was simpler. She wanted food, immediately, and she was eyeing the long mats laid out on the floor with visible suspicion.

"Wait," Damian said, when Paisley's father waved them toward the serving table. "Where do we pay? Nobody gave us a ticket at the door." Paisley grinned. "You don't pay. This is langar. It's a free meal, for everybody who walks in, no matter what religion they are." Damian lowered his phone. "Everybody? Even us?" "Even the mailman, if he came in," Paisley said. "Sit on the floor, eat, done." Ely looked at the mats again, this time with interest. "Free food and no chairs? This is the best place I have ever been."

Paisley had a theory she wanted to test, because last year she had been too small to be trusted with the roti basket and she suspected the rule about who could serve was simply whether you were careful, not how old you were. She carried a basket across the hall slowly, elbows tucked, walking like someone balancing a tower of books. The volunteer aunties watched her the whole way, and when she set it down without dropping a single piece of bread, one of them laughed and handed her a full basket to take to the far row. Theory confirmed. She felt like a scientist, if scientists got paid in roti.

Damian ended up on the other side of the serving table, laying warm bread onto plates as the line moved past, narrating under his breath that the meal "seemed to prolong the whole afternoon, in a good way." Ely ate three servings and then, wiping her hands on a napkin, announced that she was staying forever. Paisley was refilling the baskets a second time when Ms. Nair, her neighbor from two doors down, appeared at the front of the line. Ms. Nair raised her eyebrows at Paisley holding the bread. "So this is what you do on weekends," she said. Paisley handed her a plate and said, "Best warranty in town. Free refills forever."

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Nathaniel spread the photocopies across the table in the community centre craft room, where the smell of glue and old coffee hung in the air. His assignment for Ms. Siddiqui's civics club was to read the rights in the Canadian Charter and explain one in his own words at Friday's showcase. He had picked equality rights, section 15, because it sounded important. But when he compared the handout to the big laminated Charter poster on the wall, something did not match.

"Trace, come look at this," he said. Trace slid his chair over, chewing the end of a pencil. "The poster says the Charter came into force in 1982. But look at section 15." Nathaniel pointed at the small print beneath the heading. "It says 1985. Three years later."

"Maybe it's a typo," Trace said. "Photocopies always have typos."

Nathaniel tested that idea right away. He walked to the poster and ran his finger along the date line for each section. Sections 2 through 14, all 1982. Section 15, 1985. The same number appeared in the library copy Trace fetched from the shelf by the window, its pages cool and dusty. Two sources, same odd date, so the typo theory failed. Something else was going on.

He thought about how laws actually work, and about something his father had said when the province repaved their street a year after approving the budget. Big changes take time to set up. He tried a different idea: maybe the equality rights were switched on later on purpose. "Like governments needed time to fix their laws first," he said. "Maybe parliament asked for a delay."

Kaley, who was arranging her own flashcards on freedom of expression at the next table, looked up. "My mom works at the law library," she said. "She says section 15 came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws." She shrugged. "She made me memorize it for a quiz."

"So it's true," Nathaniel said. He copied the date into his notebook, then wrote his explanation underneath: everyone is equal under the law, and governments got three extra years to make their old laws match it. It felt like a significant discovery, small on paper but solid in his hands.

At the showcase on Friday, the craft room filled with folding chairs and parents holding paper cups of juice. When his turn came, Nathaniel stood at the front, held up the poster page, and said, "Everyone thinks the whole Charter started in 1982. One part waited until 1985." He tapped section 15 with two fingers. "Three years, just for equality."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: French political scientist Maurice Duverger observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties, an idea now called Duverger's law.
story:
Emilie spread the ballots across the library table like a card trick gone wrong. Forty little slips of paper, each marked with a vote for the pizza party, the art party, the gaming party, or the environment party. Ms. Tremblay's class had held the mock election on Friday, and the result had bothered Emilie all weekend. The gaming party had won with eighteen votes, even though twenty-two people had voted for other parties.

"Eighteen is not more than twenty-two," Emilie said, tapping the pile. "So why did they win everything?"

Adele slid into the chair across from her and picked up a ballot. "Because that's the rule Ms. Tremblay gave us. Most votes in the riding wins the seat. She called it first past the post."

"But it's weird." Emilie pulled the environmental studies book she'd carried over from the stacks, the one with the chapter on elections. She'd spent twenty minutes hunting for it, following a half-remembered thing her cousin had said at dinner. She flipped pages until she found the section on voting systems. "Look, there's another way. Proportional representation. If we did that, the pizza party with ten votes out of forty would get a quarter of the seats, and gaming with eighteen would get the biggest share, but not all of it."

Emilien arrived late, as usual, still holding his bike helmet. He dropped into the third chair and frowned at the paper piles. "Ms. Tremblay said we redo the vote tomorrow with five ridings instead of one. What are you two doing?"

"Testing something." Emilie dealt the ballots out into five imaginary ridings, eight votes each, using the corners of her notebook as boundaries. She counted the gaming votes in each little pile: six, five, four, two, one. In three of the five ridings, gaming beat every other single party, even though it never got half the votes anywhere. She wrote the totals down and pushed the paper to the middle of the table.

Adele leaned in. "So gaming wins three of five ridings with eighteen votes out of forty. Under first past the post, that's a majority of seats from a minority of votes. But if we counted proportionally, gaming would get less than half the seats and the others would get their share too."

"Right." Emilie kept reading, and then she sat back hard. "Listen to this. A French political scientist, Maurice Duverger, observed that first-past-the-post elections tend to produce two large parties." She read the sentence twice more. "Adele, think about our class. Every mock election we've ever had, the small parties got squashed. The art party got seven votes once and won nothing. Then half its voters gave up and picked pizza or gaming the next time."

Emilien spun his helmet on one finger. "That's why only the big two ever have a chance?"

"That's what the book says, and it fits what happened in our class, election after election." Emilie copied the page number onto her notes so she could cite it when she stood up in class tomorrow. "I'm going to propose we run the same ballots both ways, first past the post and proportional, and show everyone the difference side by side."

She gathered the slips into one neat stack and squared its edges against the table. Adele grinned and said, "You've been like a rudder all weekend, steering us straight at this."

Emilie laughed, but her hands were already sorting the ballots back into parties, making two fresh piles for the morning. "No party should be immune to questions," she said, "not even the winning one."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Lincoln slid the white gloves onto his hands and stared at the leather book Mr. Das had set on the foam cradle. "This is a real diary?" he whispered. "From the 1800s?" Mr. Das nodded and said only, "Handle the pages by the edges." Beside him, Diego leaned in so close his breath foged the glass of the display case nearby.

Their class project was due Friday, and the objective was simple: use one primary source to explain why a settler family would risk the Oregon Trail. Lincoln had picked a diary at random from the catalog, a thin volume kept by a farmer named only in the index as "E. Whitcomb, Ohio." The trouble was that the first twenty pages were all weather. Rain, frost, rain again. "Why would anyone write down the weather every single day?" Diego asked. Lincoln turned another page and noticed the entries change. Shorter. Angrier.

"May 10," he read aloud. "The bank took the farm. Twenty years of work, gone in a morning." He looked up. "Gone in a morning? What bank does that?" Lea, on his other side, was already flipping through her packet of photocopied pages. "There's something called the Panic of 1837," she said. "It says here it caused a long economic depression in the United States." Lincoln wrote the words down and wondered how a panic, something you feel, could take a farm away.

He had a guess, and guesses could be tested. If the Whitcombs lost their farm because of that panic, then the diary should show money trouble before it showed any talk of leaving. He went back to page one and read again, this time hunting for prices, debts, anything about cash. There it was, small as ticks on a dog: corn selling lower each month, a loan mentioned twice, a line in March about "hard times that will not lift."

"Look," he said, spreading three pages on the table so Lea and Diego could see the sequence. "The money trouble comes first. Then the bank. Then this." The last entry read, "We go west in the spring. There is land there, cheap and rich, if we can survive the road." Lincoln felt the whole thing click together like a puzzle with the last piece pressed in. The family hadn't wanted adventure. They'd been ruined, and the dangerous trail was still safer than staying.

"Now my paragraph almost writes itself," Lea said, borrowing his notes. "Mine too," said Diego, "except mine will be better." Lincoln checked the clock and began copying the May 10 entry word for word into his notebook. He decided to prioritize the bank line over the weather, since one farmer's rain was just rain, but one farmer's ruin could explain a wagon train. Mr. Das walked past, glanced at the open pages, and raised an eyebrow at the spread of evidence. "Legitimate work," he said quietly, and moved on.

Lincoln turned back to the diary, gloved fingers hovering over the faded ink. "What happened to you out there, E. Whitcomb?" he murmured. Then he copied the last line: "We go west in the spring."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Across many sports, home teams win more than half their games on average, an effect known as home advantage.
story:
The scoreboard at Riverside Park read zero to two, and Isabelle knew exactly what Arwen was going to say before she even opened her mouth. "That's four losses in a row, all away games." Arwen dropped onto the bench beside her and pulled off her shin guards. Their team, the Rockets, had lost twice at the field across town, once at the county fields, and now here at Riverside, which belonged to the Maplewood Tigers.

"Notice something?" Isabelle said, rolling the ball under her palm. "Every one of those was an away game."

Martina sat down on Isabelle's other side, still breathing hard. "So? A loss is a loss."

"It might not be." Isabelle stared across the grass at the Tigers' families folding up their lawn chairs on the sideline. The Tigers had won today, and they had won the last time the Rockets came here, and according to the standings posted at the rec center, Maplewood had won almost every home game this season. "I want to check something. Mr. Yoon keeps all the league results on that clipboard."

Mr. Yoon was their coach, and after the team gathered for the post-game huddle, Isabelle asked to borrow the clipboard for five minutes. He handed it over with a curious look. She sat on the curb and began to monitor the win-loss column for every team in the league, game by game, marking home games with a small dot. It was slow work. The acute afternoon light made the tiny handwriting hard to read, and she had to squint at each row.

"Verdict?" Arwen asked, peering over her shoulder.

"Look at this." Isabelle turned the clipboard around. "The teams playing at home win more than half their games. Every single team in the league, over the whole season. It's not just us being bad on the road. It's a pattern across all of them."

"Across soccer, or everything?" Martina asked.

"Mr. Yoon said it even has a name. Home advantage." She had overheard him saying it to another coach last week and had filed it away without understanding it. Now she understood.

"So here's my idea," Isabelle said on the bus ride back. "Next week we host Riverside. I say we test it. If home advantage is real, we should play differently, win. If we lose at home too, then it's just us."

The following Saturday, the Rockets played on their own field behind the community center, where the grass had that bare patch near the corner flag that Isabelle could navigate with her eyes closed. Her mother set up a folding chair at midfield. Martina's little brother sold lemonade. The game stayed tied until the second half, when Isabelle took a throw-in she had practiced a hundred times on that exact spot and found Arwen open in front of the net. Arwen scored. The Rockets won one to zero.

After the whistle, Arwen ran over and held up one finger. "One data point."

"Two," said Isabelle, pointing at the clipboard tucked under Mr. Yoon's arm. "We won last home game too. I'm keeping count."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Indonesia and Malaysia, the right hand is customarily used for eating and for giving or receiving things, as a sign of respect.
story:
Asher stood in Amina's doorway holding a bowl of his grandmother's potato salad and realized he had no idea what to do with his shoes. Everyone else's were lined up by the door, so he toed his off too, and Amina's mother pressed her palms together and nodded to him, which he copied, feeling clumsy but proud. Skylar was already inside, balancing a plate of samosas she'd brought, and the long table was crowded with dishes Asher couldn't name, steaming and fragrant and arranged like a treasure map he wanted to follow.

"Sit here," Amina said, patting the chair beside her. "Fair warning, my grandpa will ask you about your grades, your hobbies, and your entire family tree."

He did, and Asher did his best to answer, though he kept losing his train of thought because he was watching hands. Amina's father served himself with his right hand. Her grandfather passed the rice with his right hand. When Amina's little cousin handed a napkin across the table, she used her right hand too, even though her left was closer. Asher chewed slowly and tested a theory in his head: nobody, not once, had used their left hand for food or for giving anything. Not even the two-year-old, who got gently redirected. It wasn't an accident. It was a rule, an invisible one, and he'd nearly broken it ten minutes ago when he passed the samosas with his left.

"Um, Amina," he said quietly. "The right hand thing. Is that on purpose?"

She glanced around the table, then grinned. "My family's from Malaysia, and my dad's side grew up partly in Indonesia. Over there, we eat with the right hand, and we give and receive things with it too, out of respect." She shrugged. "Nobody told you because nobody wants to embarrass a guest."

Asher exhaled. So his theory held. When her grandfather offered him the potato salad, he reached out with his right hand and said, "Thank you, sir," and the old man's whole face brightened like a lamp switched on. He asked Asher three more questions about basketball, and Asher tried to articulate why he'd quit travel league, which was that the coach called every loss toxic and made practice miserable. He fumbled the words, but Mr. Grandfather just said, "Good coach teaches. Bad coach shouts," and Amina translated for the table and everyone laughed warmly.

Later, Skylar pulled him into the kitchen to finish the group project slide show for Mr. Hoang's class. "We still need a citation for the climate graph," she said, tapping the laptop. Asher leaned over her shoulder, and back in the dining room Amina called out, "Bring the mangoes when you're done, use your right hand, Asher," and he grabbed the bowl correctly, without even thinking about it.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Sara sat cross-legged on Talon's bedroom floor while Talon paced with her phone. "Read it again," Talon said. Sara retrieved the message from the screen and held it up. "Are you coming to my sleepover Friday? Also my mom says you can stay till Sunday if you want." Below it, Rory had answered twenty minutes ago: "Okay."

"That's it," Talon said. "One word. With a period. He's mad at me."

"Why would he be mad?"

"Because I didn't invite him to the lake thing last month. Look how short it is. It's basically a door slamming."

Sara wasn't sure a period could slam a door. She took out her own phone and typed the same word to Talon twice, once as "okay" and once as "Okay." Then she sent them, one after the other. Talon's phone buzzed twice. "Which one seems nicer?" Sara asked.

Talon frowned at the screen. The two bubbles sat there, symmetrical except for that one dot. "The first one. The second one sounds like my mom when she's counting to three."

"That's weird," Sara said. She typed period sincerity study into the search bar, and a headline came up. She read it out loud: "A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one."

"So it's not just me," Talon said. "Everyone reads the dot as mean." She dropped onto the bed. "But that still doesn't tell me if Rory's actually mad, or if he just types like a robot."

"Then we test it," Sara said. She composed a message and passed the phone over for Talon to approve: "Rory, you sound upset. Are you upset?" Talon hesitated, then hit send. They watched the screen. The typing bubble appeared, disappeared, appeared again, like something deciding whether to surface.

The reply came in three parts. "No." Then: "Why would I be upset." Then: "My screen cracked so I copy half my words from somewhere and the somewhere adds periods. I can't get them out. I AM coming Friday. I already asked my mom. She said Okay."

Talon laughed so hard she had to put the phone down. "He's been copying and pasting okay."

The doorbell rang. Talon ran to the window and looked down at the front step, where Rory stood holding a duffel bag and a cracked phone, three days early, waving up at them with his free hand. "Are you going to let me in," he called, "or not."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: The method of loci is a memory trick of linking each part of a text to a place along a familiar route, then walking that route in your mind to recall it.
story:
Hazel spread the index cards across the kitchen table, all twenty-two lines of her reading for the ceremony, and glared at them. Two weeks. In two weeks she would stand in front of her whole family and recite the passage from memory, and right now she could get through line seven before everything dissolved into mush.

"You look like the cards accused you of something," Matt said, letting himself in through the back door the way he always did. Mohamed-Amine followed, pulling off his bike helmet.

"They kind of did. I read them out loud forty times last night and this morning it's all gone." She shuffled the cards together and dealt them out again, as if a new order might trick her brain into holding on.

Mr. Petrov, who lived next door and had come over to return Hazel's mom's casserole dish, paused at the counter. "Forty times the same way?" He shook his head, but he didn't say anything else, which was his style. He just washed an apple and left them to it.

Mohamed-Arine picked up a card and read the first line aloud. "What if you split them up? Ten each, and we each quiz you?"

"That helps for a test," Hazel said, "but I have to stand there with nothing in my hands. No cards, no paper." She slumped against the counter. Last summer, at her grandmother's house, she had memorized the trail from the front gate to the creek in one afternoon, just by walking it. She could still close her eyes and see the crooked mailbox, the birch with the missing branch, the stone step, the shed, the bend where the ferns grew. She had never once forgotten which came next.

She sat up so fast she knocked over her water glass. "Wait. What if I put one line of the reading at each spot on Grandma's trail? Line one at the mailbox, line two at the birch, and so on. Then I just walk the trail in my head and pick up the lines as I go."

"Walk a trail that isn't there to remember words you can't see," Mohamed-Amine said slowly. "That's the strangest thing I've heard all week. Try it right now."

Hazel closed her eyes and put line one on the crooked mailbox. She pictured the words painted across its rusty door. Line two went on the birch, wrapped around the trunk like a ribbon. Line three on the stone step, line four on the shed door, line five at the fern bend. Then the trail ran out, so she invented the rest, pushing it on through the garden, past the porch swing, all the way to the creek, until twenty-two lines stood in twenty-two places.

"Okay," Matt said. "Now walk it. Out loud."

"Line one, at the mailbox." She kept her eyes shut. "Line two, at the birch." The birch gave her line two the way the porch steps gave her feet. By the shed she was three lines ahead of where she'd ever gotten before. At the creek, the last line arrived, whole and complete, and she opened her eyes.

"Twenty-two out of twenty-two," Mohamed-Amine said, checking the cards. "First try."

"First try with the trail," Hazel said. "It's like the route is doing the remembering for me." She gathered the cards into a neat stack and set them aside, then looked at the kitchen around her, at the fridge and the window and the old clock over the stove, and began laying lines down along a second route, one that started here, at this table, where she sat every single morning. That one, she thought, would be even more durable than Grandma's trail, because she walked it every day of her life.

"Tomorrow I'll do it standing up," she said. "No table, no cards, just me and the fridge."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fast growth during puberty often causes stretch marks, thin lines on the skin that are common and usually fade over time.
story:
Mia was marching to the bathroom to brush her teeth when she caught sight of her hips in the mirror and stopped so abruptly that she stepped on the cat's tail. "Sorry, Biscuit," she said, bending closer to the glass. There, on her skin, were three thin faint lines, pale and slightly wavy, like someone had drawn on her with the world's gentlest pen. She pulled her pajama waistband an inch lower, then higher, then spun around to check the other side. Lines there too.

"Mom!" she yelled down the hall. "Mom, come look at something, it's an emergency!"

Her mom appeared holding a stack of mail, still in her work clothes, sorting a letter into one pile and a pension statement into another. "What kind of emergency? Bleeding emergency, spider emergency, or you-found-my-hidden-chocolate emergency?"

"Skin emergency." Mia pointed at her hips. "I think something's wrong with me."

Her mom leaned in, looked for exactly two seconds, and smiled. "Those are stretch marks. They're really common during growth spurts, and they usually fade over time." She set the mail on the sink counter. "You grew almost two inches since summer. Your skin is just keeping notes."

Mia stared at her. That was the whole explanation? No medicine, no appointment, no dramatic bandaging? "So they just... go away on their own?"

"Fade," her mom corrected. "Eventually. Now can I brush my teeth before this emergency becomes mine?"

Mia stood there turning the idea over. She had been ready to interpret the lines as proof that something was broken, but maybe they were proof of the opposite: she was growing so fast her skin couldn't keep up. She grabbed her phone from her room and texted Aniyah, who had shot up four inches last year and complained constantly about her knees. "Do you have lines on your hips? Pale skinny ones."

The reply came fast. "YES. Five of them. I panicked in March and made my mom look at them with a flashlight." A second message followed: "She said the same thing yours did. Growth spurt stuff."

Mia laughed so hard Biscuit fled under the bed. In March, Aniyah had told everyone at lunch she might have a rare condition, and had made Cara google diseases until Mr. Tse confiscated Cara's phone in math. All that drama over something half the girls in their grade probably had. "We should start a club," Mia typed. "Membership requirement: mysterious hip lines."

"Club name?" Aniyah responded.

Mia thought about it, grinning at the mirror, at the three little lines she had decided were trophies instead of disasters. She typed back, "The Rapid Growth Society. First meeting at lunch. Bring your flashlight, we're comparing."

She flipped off the bathroom light and went to find snacks for tomorrow, taking the stairs two at a time just because she could.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Endowing means giving your partner a role or trait through what you say, as in 'Doctor, my arm hurts', which makes them the doctor.
story:
Lauren stood in the wings of the school auditorium, script pages crumpled in her fist, watching Mr. Mwangi mark an X in the center of the stage with blue tape. "Friday's assembly," he reminded the drama club. "Two minutes, no script. You and a partner make up a scene from nothing." Friday was three days away. Lauren had memorized lines for every play since second grade, but making something up in front of four hundred people felt like being asked to jump off a diving board without water in the pool.

She tried it first with Ali after school. "Okay," Lauren said, "we're in a kitchen." Ali crossed his arms. "Why are we in a kitchen?" Nothing happened after that. They stood there until the bell rang. On the walk home, Lauren wondered what had gone wrong, and she began to suspect the trouble wasn't the kitchen at all. It was that neither of them knew who the other one was supposed to be.

The next day she watched Gabryel and a sixth grader run a scene. The sixth grader froze, mouth open, hands dangling. Then Gabryel grabbed her sleeve and shouted, "Captain, the engine room is flooding!" The girl straightened up like a string had pulled her spine, and suddenly she was the captain, barking orders about the pumps. How did that work? Lauren hadn't seen anything change except the word "Captain." She started keeping a list in her notebook of moments like that, and a pattern appeared: whenever someone gave their partner a name or a job out loud, the partner stopped being stuck.

She found Mr. Mwangi after lunch and asked why it worked. He only grinned and said, "It's called endowing," then walked off to find his clipboard. Endowing. Giving your partner a role through what you say. That night she tested it at dinner, telling her mother, "Nurse, my arm hurts," and her mother, without missing a beat, examined the arm and diagnosed an allergy to broccoli. Lauren laughed so hard she nearly fell off her chair. It worked on people who didn't even know they were playing.

At Thursday's rehearsal she partnered with Ali again, and this time she had a plan. She walked on stage, peered at him, and said, "Yes, and I see you're the doctor here, Doctor Ali. My arm hurts." Ali wobbled for half a second, then grabbed an imaginary stethoscope. "Yes, and I'm afraid it's serious. Nurse!" he called, pointing at Lauren. "Yes, and this nurse is completely impartial," she announced, "so you can trust my diagnosis," and she declared that the cure was a dance. They danced. Mr. Mwangi clapped from the third row.

On Friday, under the hot stage lights, Lauren felt her knees go wobbly as four hundred faces looked up at her. Then she took a breath, looked straight at Ali, and said, "Captain, the asteroid is coming."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: The cell wall is the thick outer border you see around each onion cell, making the cells look like rows of bricks.
story:
Evan had one class period to draw a diagram nobody in his family would believe he made. Mr. Bouchard had announced that whoever labeled the cell wall, the membrane and the nucleus correctly on their onion slide would get full marks, and Evan's grade in science had begun to deteriorate after the broken graduated cylinder incident in October. This diagram was his chance to fix that.

He peeled the papery skin off the onion slice with tweezers, laid it flat in a drop of water on the slide, and pressed the coverslip down. Through the eyepiece at first all he saw was a gray smear, so he turned the coarse focus one small notch at a time until the smear sharpened into rows of boxes, packed edge to edge, like bricks in a wall.

"Mine's broken," said Melody at the next station. "I think I put a piece of brick wall on my slide somehow. Look, there are mortar lines and everything." She was laughing, but not really, the way people laugh when they're afraid they've ruined their only chance at a mark.

Evan looked over at her slide. The same rows of boxes. He looked back at his own. "Bricks don't come off an onion," he said slowly. "I peeled that skin off with tweezers. It was one thin sheet." He held up the tweezers. "So each of those boxes has to be one cell. The thick outer border around every single box, that's the cell wall. That's why they look like rows of bricks."

Melody stared into her microscope for a long moment. "So the 'mortar' is just the walls," she said. "Then the membrane must be the thin line right inside it, and that darker blob in the middle of each one is the nucleus." She began drawing fast, her pencil scratching out box after box.

Evan copied the idea carefully, but he wanted to be sure the nucleus wasn't just a bubble or a speck of dirt. He remembered that Mr. Bouchard had mentioned the stain bottle at the front bench, so he borrowed a drop of iodine, added it to the edge of his coverslip, and watched it seep under. Every blob in every box darkened at once. Real structures then, not dirt. Dirt wouldn't appear in each cell like a pattern.

He labeled his drawing and added a title in careful letters. Melody leaned over. "Write my name on yours too," she said, "since you basically just saved my grade in front of the whole class."

Mr. Bouchard stopped at their bench, picked up Evan's diagram, and held it up so the iodine stain on the paper caught the light. "Rows of bricks," he said, and set it back down with a small nod.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Cats are obligate carnivores, which means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet.
story:
On Saturday morning Daniel stood in front of the cat cages at the shelter with his adoption paperwork half filled out, and one box stopped him cold: "What will you feed this animal?" He was a vegetarian, like his whole family, and he had assumed a kitten could eat what they ate. The shelter closed at five, and he had until then to prove he could care for the small gray cat he'd already named Pesto.

Maddison and Emaan had come along for the trip, and they crowded around the cage while Daniel looked at Pesto's chart. "It says here he's a domestic shorthair," Emaan said. "That's not one of those hereditary fancy breeds, right? So no special medical stuff?"

"It just means his family tree is ordinary," Daniel said. Then he frowned at the chart again. "But there's something about diet." He carried the paper to the corner where the shelter kept display bags of food and started reading labels, flipping one bag over after another. Every single one listed chicken, fish, or turkey as the first ingredient. Not one was meat-free. That felt like a clue, a pattern he couldn't ignore.

Maddison pulled out her phone. "I'll look it up if you want." She typed, then read slowly. "It says cats are obligate carnivores." She held up the screen. "It means they depend on nutrients found in animal flesh and they cannot stay healthy on a vegetarian diet."

Daniel sat down on the bench, and for a minute he didn't say anything. His allowance came out of his income from mowing lawns, and he'd been planning to spend it on toys and treats, not a separate kind of food the rest of the family would never touch. It felt strange to buy meat for a house with none in it. But if he didn't, Pesto would get sick, and Daniel had already signed his name in pen on the line that said "responsible owner."

He thought of an experiment to test the idea. In the meet-and-greet room he set out two bowls, one with the shelter's meat-based kibble and one with the lentil stew his mom had packed for his own lunch. He put them side by side and let Pesto choose. The kitten sniffed the stew, wrinkled his nose, and buried the whole bowl under the rubber mat like it was garbage. Then he crunched through the kibble until the bowl was dry.

"Well," Daniel said, laughing, "that's pretty clear." He went back to the front desk, asked Ms. Tran for the biggest bag of cat food they sold, and set it beside his backpack. When Pesto mewed from the carrier, Daniel leaned down and said, "Don't worry. Lentils are never happening again."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
The car smelled like the pine air freshener Dad refused to throw away, which he claimed he kept to preserve the memories of every road trip they'd ever taken, and which Evelyn privately thought just preserved the smell of old french fries.

"You've been staring at your shoes for ten minutes," Dad said, glancing at her in the mirror. "The shoes are fine. The dance will be fine."

"It's not the shoes." Evelyn pulled her knees up onto the seat. "It's the dancing part. Everybody will be dancing and I'll just be standing by the punch table holding a cup."

In the back of her mind she replayed yesterday, when she'd been at Payton's house pretending to work on their science homework. Payton had got distracted, as usual, and pulled up a video on her laptop. "Forget people," Payton had said, spinning the screen around. "Watch this bird." It was a sulphur-crested cockatoo called Snowball, bobbing and stepping to a song, actually in time with the beat. Payton, who wanted to be an entrepreneur someday and narrated everything like a pitch, had added, "In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed Snowball could keep time to music. When they sped the song up, he sped up too." Evelyn had watched it three times. If a bird could hear a tempo and adjust, she'd thought, then keeping a beat wasn't some mysterious talent you were born with. It was something you could notice, and copy, and practice. She'd tested the idea in her bedroom last night with her headphones on, finding the beat in each song, tapping her foot, stepping side to side. It hadn't felt like magic. It had felt like a rule she could follow.

Estelle's house was the next stop, and Estelle climbed in with a bag of hair clips and zero hesitation. "I have a plan," she announced. "We stand near the speakers so we can feel the beat in the floor, and we dance near the wall so nobody can get behind us. Genius, right?"

"Best songs are subjective anyway," Estelle added, buckling her seatbelt. "So even if the DJ plays something terrible, we can still find the beat. It's in there somewhere."

Evelyn smiled. "Can I tell you guys something? I practiced. In my room. Because of a cockatoo."

"A what?" Dad said.

"A bird on the internet. If he can keep the beat, I figure I can too."

Dad pulled up in front of the gym, where the doors glowed yellow and the bass thumped through the concrete. Evelyn took a breath, grabbed Estelle's arm, and said, "Let's go find the speakers."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: All 50 U.S. states, and Washington, D.C., have passed laws on handling concussions in youth sports.
story:
Eleanor had been practicing her crossover for six weeks, and now the ball bounced off her knee and rolled all the way to the fence. Tryouts for the school basketball team were thirty minutes in, and so far she had missed two layups, one free throw, and a pass to a girl who wasn't even looking.

"You're rushing it," said Kellan, jogging past with a water bottle. "You play like the ball owes you money."

"I play like the ball is trying to escape," Eleanor said, and chased it down.

Mr. Chaudhry, the coach, blew his whistle and set up a scrimmage. Eleanor got the ball at the top of the key, faked left like she'd practiced against the garage door a hundred times, and drove. Yasser, guarding her, reached in, and their feet tangled. She hit the floor hard, the back of her head kissing the wood with a sound she felt more than heard.

She stood up fast, because standing up fast was what she'd always done. The gym had a strange shine to it, like someone had polished the lights.

"Eleanor." Mr. Chaudhry was suddenly in front of her, holding her elbow. "Sit down on the bench. You're done for today."

"I'm fine," she said. "I get dizzy when I'm nervous anyway."

"You took a hit to the head. Sit."

On the bench, Kellan sat beside her while Yasser brought her water and apologized four separate times. Eleanor watched the scrimmage, furious, then confused, then thinking. The coach had pulled two other kids over the years, she remembered, always after head knocks, never for twisted ankles or bleeding elbows. It wasn't just his personal caution. There was a rule behind it, a pattern she couldn't see, like wind you only know by the leaves.

"Is it school policy?" she asked Mr. Chaudhry during the water break. "Pulling people after they hit their heads?"

"It's the law," he said. "Every state has one, all fifty plus Washington, D.C. There's no version of this where I let you back in today."

"Wait, the actual law?" said Kellan. "Like, with police?"

"With paperwork," said Mr. Chaudhry, and jogged back to the scrimmage.

Eleanor sat with that. A law, written down somewhere, protecting her from her own fastest instinct, which was to say she was fine. It felt like discovering the court had a foundation under it, something solid she'd been standing on without knowing. She tested the idea against what she'd seen: kids pulled for head hits, never for anything else, at every school game she could remember. It fit.

She sustained a headache through the rest of tryouts, and the next day her mother took her to a doctor who signed a form, because that was part of the law too. On Thursday, Mr. Chaudhry posted the roster. Eleanor made the second list, the practice squad, one spot below Yasser.

"You got cut and not cut," Kellan said. "Schrodinger's teammate."

Eleanor grinned and pulled on her sneakers. At the first practice, when Mr. Chaudhry called for someone assertive on defense, she raised her hand so fast it nearly hit Yasser in the chin.

"Careful," he said, ducking. "That could be against the law too."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: The turnaround is the end of the twelve-bar form, usually landing on the V chord, which pulls the music back to the start of the next chorus.
story:
The community centre's basement smelled of old carpet and burnt coffee, and every Thursday it turned into a blues jam run by Ms. Kovalenko. Asher stood at the edge of the room with his borrowed guitar, watching the older players take turns soloing over the twelve-bar progression. He had practised the scale until his fingers were agile enough to find every note without looking, but tonight Ms. Kovalenko had pointed at him and said, "You're in on the next chorus." Now he was terrified.

"Count the bars," Arian whispered from behind the keyboard. "Four on each chord. When it comes back around, you'll hear it."

Arian's sister Maika started the drums with a steady shuffle, and the whole room leaned into the groove. Asher played his first phrase, then a second, elaborating on the little three-note motif he had rehearsed all week. It sounded almost like the blues. Then somewhere around the seventh bar he stopped counting. His mind went blank, and his fingers kept moving while the chords shifted underneath him like floorboards sliding out of place. He was lost. He had no idea where he was in the form, and he could feel his ears getting hot.

Then he noticed something. The bass walked upward, the keyboard changed, and the whole band seemed to gather itself, like a scavenger spotting the same prize from across the field, everyone turning toward one point. The music climbed and settled, and a moment later the progression started over from the beginning, exactly where it had begun. He had heard that move a hundred times on recordings without ever really hearing it. That was it, the signpost.

"That's the turnaround," Arian said after the tune ended. "End of the form. Lands on the five chord and pulls you right back to the top."

"Does it always?" Asher asked.

"Pretty much. It's how lost soloists find home."

They played two more choruses, and once more Asher lost his place when Maika flipped her drum pattern and threw him off. This time he didn't panic. He hung on a couple of safe notes like a kid treading water, listened for the band to gather and climb, and when he heard the pull back toward the beginning he leapt. His next phrase landed right on the first chord, loud and sure, and Arian grinned across the keyboards.

Ms. Kovalenko raised her coffee cup toward him from her chair by the amplifier and said, "Again from the top."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: Many blues songs use a shuffle rhythm, in which each pair of eighth notes is played long-short instead of evenly.
story:
Aiden had learned the twelve-bar progression in one afternoon, which felt like a victory until he actually played it. The chords were right, the notes of his solo were right, and somehow the whole thing sounded like a microwave beeping. Keagan was coming over at four o'clock to hear the solo, because Keagan had already promised the whole lunch table that Aiden would play it at the talent show sign-up on Friday. That gave Aiden two hours to sound like music instead of a robot.

He played the progression again and listened hard. The notes were correct; he was sure of that. His fingers knew where to go. The problem was something else, something hiding under the notes where he couldn't see it, like the way a floor can look level until a marble rolls to one side. He tried playing louder. He tried playing faster. He tried closing his eyes, which only made him think about how little time was left. His mom called from the kitchen that if he was going to persevere, could he at least persevere more quietly.

Then he put on an old blues track Ms. Vargas had lent him and tapped his foot along. His foot kept wanting to land in the wrong places, splitting some beats and squashing others, and he stopped the song and rewound it twice. He tapped again, clapping each pair of eighth notes instead of the big beats. Long-short. Long-short. Every single pair, long-short, never even. "It's a shuffle," he said out loud to the piano, feeling slightly ridiculous. "The eighth notes are long-short, not even." He had been playing the solo as if the notes were all the same length, and the stiffness hadn't been in his fingers at all. It had been an illusion that playing the right notes meant playing the right rhythm.

He tried it. On the first pass he overshot, so swung that he crashed into the next chord like a shopper with a full cart. The second pass was better. By the fourth pass something happened that he couldn't quite account for: the solo started walking, then limping in an interesting way, and the twelve bars went by before he noticed them. It sounded, for about six seconds, like actual blues. He played it again to make sure he hadn't imagined it.

At four o'clock Keagan let himself in through the back door, as usual, and dropped onto the piano bench. "Okay, disaster check. Can you actually do this by Friday?" Aiden set his hands on the keys and started the progression, long-short, long-short, letting the last note of the solo hang there a little longer than it should have, the way the recording did. Keagan stopped chewing his gum. "Wait. Do that again."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
story:
Luke sat in the waiting room of Dr. Patel's office, holding his elbow because his mom had insisted he needed "a check on the sniffles," which was embarrassing enough without Jerry spotting him there. Of course Jerry spotted him there. Jerry was in the corner chair with an ice pack on his wrist from a skateboard attempt he refused to describe.

"Coach says you're starting in Thursday's game," Jerry said, grinning even as he shifted the ice pack. "You excited? Because I told everyone you'd do a victory flip if we win, so that's happening now. Voluntary or not."

"That was voluntary when you promised it. Now it's a trap," Luke said, but he was grinning too. Starting was huge news. He leaned back, then caught a whiff of himself and sat forward again fast. Since when did he smell like a locker room? He'd never needed deodorant before this year, and today he'd forgotten it entirely after gym.

He turned the problem over while a toddler across the room mimic-kicked a soccer ball, narrating her own goal. Fresh sweat couldn't be the culprit, could it? He'd been practically dry after gym, right up until he wasn't. He remembered his older cousin rambling at Thanksgiving: "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. The smell comes when bacteria on your skin break down the sweat from your armpit glands, and those glands kick in at puberty." At the time Luke had nodded the way you nod at relatives. Now it felt like classified information. The pattern fit. New glands, new bacteria buffet, new smell, all starting months ago exactly when his voice went sideways.

So he tested it. He sneaked to the drinking fountain, wet a paper towel, and scrubbed one armpit like it owed him money, leaving the other one as what Cynthia would call the control group, if Cynthia were there, which thankfully she was not. Five minutes later he sniffed each side. The scrubbed side smelled like damp paper towel. The other side smelled like a science experiment. It worked. The bacteria were the problem, and soap was the answer. Probability of him carrying wipes in his gym bag from now on: extremely high.

"Luuuuke," the nurse called.

He stood up so fast he knocked a magazine off the table, and Jerry howled. "Dude, you're more nervous about a checkup than a game."

"I'm not nervous," Luke said, and then, because he couldn't resist telling anyone, "I just solved body odor with a paper towel."

"Put that on the team group chat," Jerry said immediately. "Coach will make you captain for science."

The nurse held the door open and raised an eyebrow at the damp towel in Luke's hand.

"Medical research," Luke told her, and marched in.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
Keira counted the boxes in the moving truck one last time, then climbed into the back seat. Her father had taken the new job with a corporation two states away, and no amount of arguing about it in June had changed anything by August. Mael had promised to text every day, and for the first week he actually did.

At her new school, Ms. Li stood at the door on the first morning, distributing schedules to the line of sixth graders. Keira took hers and found a seat near the window. At lunch she stood alone with her tray until a girl named Alexanne waved her over. They ate together, and Alexanne talked the whole time about the soccer team and a science project that involved something volatile that they weren't allowed to touch without goggles. Keira laughed in the right places. Afterward, walking to class, she caught herself thinking that Alexanne was her friend now, and then she thought about Mael, and about how many lunches it had taken with him before she would have told him a secret. Something didn't add up.

That night she searched on her mom's laptop until she found it. A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas had found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. She read the sentence twice, then did the math on a sticky note. Lunch was thirty minutes. Fifty hours was one hundred lunches. Almost an entire school year, if you counted nothing but lunch.

So she tested it. The next day she sat with Alexanne again, and the day after that, and she started keeping a tally in the back of her notebook, a small pencil mark for every half hour. She joined the soccer team because Alexanne was on it, which added two hours of practice most days. Some afternoons Alexanne barely talked to her, and Keira marked the hours anyway, the way you mark rainy days in a garden and keep watering.

Near the end of October, Alexanne knocked on her door holding two bus passes. "My mom got extras for the science museum," she said. "Want to come Saturday? It's like four hours, more if we get lost."

Keira looked at her tally page, then folded it in half and shoved it in a drawer. Four hours was four hours, but she was pretty sure they'd already stopped counting.

"Only if we get lost on purpose," she said, grabbing her jacket.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
Israel's basement smelled like old carpet and microwave popcorn. He rolled his desk chair sideways so Jackson could reach the second keyboard, and Sky dropped onto the couch with her notebook already open.

"Okay," Israel said. "You said you'd write it yourself. A program that asks for a number and prints whether it's prime. I'm not touching the keyboard."

Jackson cracked his knuckles and typed. He decomposed the problem in his head the way Ms. Qureshi had shown them in math: get the number, then check whether anything divides it, then print the answer. One step at a time. He wrote a loop that tried every number from 2 up to the input, and if it found one that divided evenly, it printed "not prime." Otherwise, after the loop finished, it printed "prime."

"Run it," Sky said, chewing her pen.

He typed 9. The screen said not prime. He typed 7. Prime. He typed 25, 13, 100, 41. Every answer was right. Sky leaned over and frowned at the screen.

"Try 2," she said. "Small numbers are where programs mess up."

He typed 2. The screen said not prime. Jackson sat back. That was wrong, and he knew it, but he couldn't see why. The loop seemed airtight. He read the code line by line, twice, and it looked plausible to him, every part of it.

"Wait," he said slowly. "The loop starts at 2. So for the input 2, the loop divides 2 by 2, it comes out even, and it says not prime. It's testing the number against itself." He highlighted the line. "But for prime, the number only counts if something smaller divides it." He changed the loop to stop before it reached the input itself.

"It's like the loop had a hierarchy problem," he said. "The number itself was sneaking into the check when it shouldn't."

Israel typed 2. The screen said prime. Then he typed 4. Not prime. 6, not prime. 8, not prime. He started typing every even number he could think of, and every single one came back not prime, until he got bored and typed 2 again just to watch it say prime.

"That's weird," Israel said. "It's the only even one that ever says prime."

"That's not the program being weird," Sky said. "That's real. 2 is the only even prime number."

"So every other even number is out," Jackson said, almost to himself. He added one line at the top of the check: if the number is even and bigger than 2, skip everything and print not prime. The program barely had to work at all now. He ran it on 100, and it answered before the rest of the loop even started.

"You just made the program faster by knowing the math," Israel said. "That feels like cheating."

Jackson saved the file under his own name. The screen blinked, and beneath it a new message appeared: one unread email from Ms. Qureshi, forwarded from Israel's account. Subject line: "Extra credit, due Monday."

"You had it the whole time?" Jackson said.

Israel grinned and hit send.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A percentage based on very few attempts can be misleading: a player who makes one shot out of one attempt shoots 100 percent.
story:
Anna slid her basketball stats sheet under her brother's elbow and reached for the mashed potatoes before her mom could distribute them unevenly again. Her dad was already halfway through his chicken, but Anna barely touched hers.

"Loik says he's the best shooter on our team," she said. "He's been telling everyone in the hallway. He was explicit about it, too. One shot, one basket. One hundred percent."

"One hundred percent," her dad repeated, raising his eyebrows. "That's impressive."

"It's one shot." Anna stabbed a green bean. "The whole season. He played two minutes in one game because three people were out sick, and he took one shot, and it went in. Now he's got this perfect percentage and he's saying Amirah should come off the bench instead of him."

Her mom set down her fork. "What's Amirah's percentage?"

"That's the thing." Anna pulled the napkin from her lap and turned it over. "She's taken like forty shots and made twenty-three. I did the division twice. It's a little over fifty percent, and she doesn't even play guard, so most of her shots are hard ones." She wrote 23/40 on the napkin, then 1/1 next to it. "Fifty-something sounds worse than a hundred, if you just read the numbers out loud."

Her brother leaned over to look. "So Loik wins."

"Loik wins on a number that means nothing." Anna tapped the napkin. "It felt like a paradox when I first worked it out, because the numbers say one thing and the truth says another. But it's not really a paradox. It's just a small amount of information pretending to be a big one." She chewed her lip. "The problem is that the number itself isn't wrong, so I can't just tell him he's lying."

"So what are you going to do?" her mom asked.

Anna was quiet for a moment, pushing a pea around her plate. Then she sat up straight. "I'm going to get him to take more shots. We have shooting practice before Thursday's game, the kind where Coach writes down everything. If Loik takes ten shots, the number will fix itself, whatever it turns out to be. And if he really is the best shooter, then fine, he gets to brag with an actual number behind it." She folded the napkin and put it in her pocket. "Either way, the truth shows up."

"Even if he misses all ten?" her brother asked.

"Then he's a one-for-eleven shooter who talks too much." Anna grinned and finally took a real bite of chicken. "And I'm going to text Amirah right after dinner so she can count the shots with me."

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: In jazz and blues jams, players often 'trade fours', taking turns to improvise four bars each.
story:
Emilie counted under her breath while the backing track looped through the twelve bars for the ninth time. She could play the chords fine, A7, D7, A7, E7, but every time she tried to solo her notes came out stiff, like she was reading them off an invisible list. She wanted her guitar to answer the music, not just stand next to it.

She texted Taya, who had been playing saxophone for two years, and recruited her for an experiment. "Bring your sax," Emilie typed. "I have a theory." Taya arrived within the hour, socks mismatched as usual, and they set up in Emilie's living room with the backing track on the speaker.

"Play something," Emilie said, "and I'll copy it back at you, like a conversation." Taya blew a bendy phrase that slid down like water off a roof. Emilie tried to answer on guitar and it fell flat, too many notes, no shape. She stopped the track. Why had Taya's four seconds of music sounded like a sentence and hers sounded like a spill? She wondered if the problem was invisible, something about the length of the phrase rather than the notes themselves.
