They tried again, but this time Emilie counted the bars while Taya played. One, two, three, four, and then it was Emilie's turn, four more bars, back and forth like a tennis rally. She picked one small candidate phrase, three notes that bent, and let it repeat and stretch, elastic, changing a little each time it came around. When Taya answered with a sassy little scooping riff, Emilie answered that instead of her own idea, and suddenly the music sounded like two people talking.

"That's a real thing, you know," Taya said between takes. "It's called trading fours." They grinned at each other and started the track again. This time Emilie didn't plan anything. She listened, counted, and when her four bars came she let her guitar ask a question she didn't know the answer to yet. Taya's saxophone replied with a low growl, and Emilie chased it back up the neck, landing on the one note that felt like a period at the end of a sentence.

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under first-past-the-post, two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, letting a third candidate win with fewer votes than their combined total.
story:
Luke spread the ballot slips across the kitchen table, forty little squares of paper he had talked Ms. Doyle into letting him count twice. The class election was over, and Skylar had lost, which was strange, because Skylar and Kassandra had promised almost exactly the same things: longer recess, a suggestion box, a class pet. He was supposed to be finishing a book report where the protagonist survived a blizzard, but the numbers bothered him more.

He counted the way the election had actually gone. Skylar got twelve votes, Kassandra got ten, and a boy whose entire speech had been "vote for me, I'm fun" got eighteen. Skylar and Kassandra had been chronic allies all year, sitting together, agreeing on everything, and together their supporters added up to twenty-two. That was more than eighteen. Luke stacked the slips into three piles and stared at them.

Kassandra arrived first, dumping her backpack on a chair. "I came to complain," she announced. "That's basically my hobby now."

"Look," Luke said, and slid the piles toward her. "The way our election works, whoever gets the most votes wins. It doesn't matter that your votes and Skylar's votes were for nearly the same ideas."

Skylar came through the back door without knocking, which was usual. "Ms. Doyle said you took the ballots."

"Only to count them," Luke said. "Here." He pushed the piles together, then split them a different way. "Pretend you two had been one candidate. Same platform, one name. Twenty-two votes. Fun Guy gets eighteen. You win." He rebuilt the original piles. "Split, he wins. Same people, same votes, different result."

Skylar picked up the winning pile, eighteen slips, and weighed it in her hand. "So being similar to Kassandra is what lost it for me."

"Basically, yes." Luke had spent an hour trying to find some hidden trick in the counting, some mistake, and there wasn't one. The count was clean. The rule itself did it.

"I assumed Kassandra stole my ideas," Skylar said slowly. "I was going to be mad about it all term." She set the pile down. "I'm not, now. It wasn't her."

"There's another way to count," Luke said, pulling over his notebook. He had copied a system from the encyclopedia: if you share out the seats according to each side's share of the votes, it's called proportional representation. "If we ran the class that way, your ideas would still get a voice, because your votes would count toward something." He wrote out a sample count with make-believe numbers so Kassandra could see it work.

Kassandra leaned over the notebook, tapping the page. "So we take this to Ms. Doyle."

"For the next vote," Skylar said. "Not to redo this one. Rules are rules, even bad ones." She was already grinning, though. "But next time, we don't split."

"Or we run on completely different platforms," Kassandra said.

"Or that," Skylar said, and scooped the ballots back into the envelope to return them first thing in the morning.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
story:
Clara sat in her grandmother's kitchen with the laptop propped on a stack of cookbooks, because Grandma's Wi-Fi only worked near the window. The program was supposed to be simple. Ask for a number, test it, print whether it was prime. Mr. Weiss had told the class that primes were the fundamental building blocks of numbers, and that they had to write a checker by Sunday. So far, Clara's checker insisted that seven was not prime, thirteen was not prime, and even three was not prime.

"They can't all be not prime," Lyvia said from the phone, leaning against her video call screen. "Three is definitely prime. I'd bet my lunch on it."

"Then my code is calling my lunch," Clara muttered. She scrolled through it again. Ask for the number. Then, for every possible divisor from two up through the number itself, divide and check. She had written it with a while loop that counted all the way up to n, dividing by n at the end.

A memory surfaced from Tuesday. Mr. Weiss had stood by the whiteboard and said, almost offhandedly, "Careful with ranges in Python, everyone. Range of two and n gives you the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1." Then the fire alarm went off for a drill, and everyone had filed outside, sneezing in the pollen, and Clara had never written the rest down. She had assumed she remembered it anyway.

She stared at her loop now, heart tapping a little faster. Her loop divided n by n at the end. Every number divided by itself. Every number got stamped not prime. Her program wasn't broken exactly; it was answering a different question than the one she'd asked.

She deleted the while loop and typed the fix, using range with two and n, her fingers slow and deliberate. She pressed enter. She typed seven. Prime. Eleven. Prime. Eight. Not prime. She was about to shout for Lyvia when a shadow fell across the keyboard.

Grandma stood there with her tea, reading the screen. "You'll want to compress that loop," she said. "One flag variable instead of all those prints."

Clara froze. "You know Python?"

"Python's new to me," Grandma said mildly. "Loops aren't. I wrote payroll code before your father was born, and I still remember the day a range cost me a week." She set down her cup and pulled a chair up beside Clara. "Show me the allergy you wrote for the number one."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs break down very slowly, and dark or baking chocolate is far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate.
story:
Daniel had saved for eleven weeks, and today the pet store was letting him carry out a small brown puppy with one ear that flopped the wrong way. Inara came along to help choose supplies, and she held the list he had written while he counted money at the register.

"Food bowl, leash, puppy kibble," she read. "You forgot treats."

"Did not. Treats are right there." Daniel pointed at a shelf, and while he paid, the cashier slipped a small milk chocolate bar into the bag. "On the house," she said. "For the new owner, not the dog." Daniel laughed and forgot about it.

At home, he set the puppy, Biscuit, on the kitchen floor while he sorted supplies. Biscuit was diligent about one thing above all: finding anything edible. When Daniel turned around, the pup was dragging a paper bag off the counter's edge, and chocolate chips were scattering across the tiles like dark hail. It was baking chocolate, the bag his mother kept for cookies, and Biscuit had already swallowed a mouthful.

Daniel's stomach dropped. He remembered the cashier's joke and thought, it was a joke, so chocolate must be bad, but how bad? A milk chocolate bar versus a bag of baking chocolate did not feel like the same problem. He grabbed the chip bag and called Inara, who looked it up while he watched Biscuit's tail wag, oblivious.

"You have to call the vet," she said. "It says dogs break down something in chocolate really slowly, so it stays in them a long time. And dark or baking chocolate is way more dangerous than milk chocolate."

"The bag calls it theobromine," Daniel said, reading the label with a frown.

Mr. Navarro, the neighbour across the hall, knocked at the sound of the phone call and drove them straight to the clinic, because Daniel's mother would not be home for an hour and the vet said not to wait. In the waiting room, Daniel kept his hand on Biscuit's crate. The vet treated Biscuit, and by evening the puppy was sleepy but fine, curled in a towel-lined box.

At school the next day, Malek asked why Daniel looked so tired. "Biscuit ate baking chocolate," Daniel said. "Milk chocolate would have been less dangerous, but baking chocolate is the worst kind, because of the theobromine. Dogs break it down really slowly." He wrote a note and taped it to the kitchen cabinet at home, right beside the flour: NO CHOCOLATE ANYWHERE BISCUIT CAN REACH.

He also did one more thing. He went back to the pet store, found the cashier, and asked her to trade the joke for a bag of puppy biscuits. "Fair enough," she said, ringing it up. That night Biscuit sat at his feet, ears up, watching him open the bag.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
On Saturday morning, a small box sat beside Chloe's cereal bowl with her name on it. Her mom grinned and said, "Happy birthday, almost." Inside was a phone, dark blue and shiny, and Chloe actually shrieked. She spent the whole day taking pictures of the toaster, the cat, and her own sneakers, and by nine that night she was still in bed under her blanket, scrolling through videos with the brightness turned up.

The next morning she dragged herself to the bus stop like her backpack was full of bricks. Averie took one look at her and said, "You look like a zombie." Chloe yawned so hard her jaw cracked. The weird part was that this had happened before, at her cousin's house last summer, when she and Jessy had stayed up past midnight with Jessy's tablet. Chloe remembered lying on the air mattress, eyes wide open, listening to Jessy snore while her own brain refused to shut off. On nights she read paper books instead, she dropped off almost instantly. Both times she'd been tired. Only one variable was different.

At lunch she laid it out for Averie and Jessy like a detective. "Nights with screens, I can't sleep. Nights without, I can. I want to test it properly." She borrowed a notebook from Ms. Charles's classroom shelf and made a chart: five nights, phone off and in the kitchen before bed, and a note each morning about how fast she fell asleep. Her motivation was simple and enormous: the school camping trip was in two weeks, and she did not want to be the kid who lay awake in a tent listening to everyone else breathe.

Night one, she left the phone downstairs and felt like part of her arm was missing. But she was asleep in what felt like ten minutes. Night two, same. Night three, same, and she wrote "wow" in the margin with three exclamation points. Then came the twist. On night four her dad knocked on her door holding the phone. "You left this on the couch," he said. "And I looked something up, because your mom was curious." He read off his own phone: "Blue-enriched light from screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin."

"Melatonin," Chloe repeated. "That's the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening." She said it slowly, like the word was the missing puzzle piece, because it was. It wasn't the videos, it wasn't sinister screen plots to ruin her life, it was light with a lot of blue in it telling her body to postpone sleepiness. She finished night five, and her chart showed five quick fall-asleeps in a row, plus one zombie week before it for comparison.

At the campsite, in her sleeping bag with a headlamp that glowed warm yellow, Chloe propped the notebook open on her knees. Jessy leaned over from the next mattress pad and whispered, "What are you writing?" Chloe showed her the chart and clicked off the lamp. "Rule one," she said. "The phone sleeps in the tent pocket."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge, and short bursts of it can help a person focus, such as before a test or a race.
story:
Luke sat on his bedroom floor with his spelling list in one hand and his science poster in the other, and his heart would not stop hammering. The poster showed a bee drifting from flower to flower, and across the bottom, in his best lettering, he had written that bees pollinate the apple trees behind Ms. Levy's garden, which was why her branches sagged with fruit every September. He could not make himself study it. Tomorrow was the thing he was not saying out loud, even to himself, and it sat in his chest like a stone.

His phone buzzed. Quentin had sent a message: "Still freaking out? Lionel says use your coping list." Luke typed back "working on it," then stared at the list he'd taped to his wall weeks ago, back when his mom first used the word anxiety at the doctor's office. Deep breaths. Count backward. Set boundaries on worrying, which meant picking one worry time and refusing the rest. He had tried all of it. His hands were still cold, and the bee poster still looked like a smudge.

Then he noticed something odd. He had read the paragraph about bees three times without remembering a word, but when the clock ticked closer to nine, when his worry got acute enough that he could hear the radiator clicking in the corner, he suddenly caught an error he had missed all evening. He had written that flowers pollinate bees. Backwards. His sharpened attention had spotted it instantly, the same way he could hear his dad's van on the street before anyone else did. Luke set down the marker. Maybe the hammering in his chest was not only an enemy.

He decided to test it, because that was what you did with a pattern you weren't sure of. He copied five hard spelling words while calm, breathing slow, keeping the worry behind a boundary. He got two wrong. Then he let himself think about tomorrow on purpose, let the nerves come roaring up, and copied five more. He got all five right. He did it again with the poster facts, and again the worry made his mind grab every detail, quick and tight. His phone buzzed a second time, and this time he answered it out loud.

"Quentin, listen. Stress is the body's response to a demand or challenge," Luke said, reading straight off the health worksheet that had been buried under his poster all night. "It says short bursts of it can actually help you focus. Like before a test." There was a pause on the line.

"So your freak-out is doing your homework for you?"

"Basically. Quentin," Luke said, and took the breath he'd been holding since dinner. "Tomorrow's my trumpet solo in front of the whole school. First row of the band, all by myself." The phone was quiet for so long that the radiator clicked twice. Then Luke picked up the trumpet case from under his bed, snapped the latches open, and raised the mouthpiece to his lips.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark.
story:
Mason had six cups of mystery liquid lined on the science fair table, and no idea what was in any of them. Ms. Mansour had labeled them only A through F, shaken each one, and said, "Test them. Tell me acid or base." His palms began to perspire as the first visitors drifted toward his booth.

"We're supposed to dip the litmus paper," his friend Eden reminded him, holding out the little strip of blue paper. "You're just staring at the cups."

"I'm thinking." Mason took the strip and dipped it into cup A. The paper turned pink. He wrote it down, dipped a fresh strip into cup B, and watched that one stay blue. Cup C turned pink so fast the change seemed to snap across the paper like a spark.

Oakley leaned over the table. "So pink means acid, blue means base. Then what's cup D?"

Mason dipped a strip. It stayed blue. He frowned at it. "Base. But Ms. Mansour said something about a scale, the pH scale. She said acids are at the low end and bases at the high end, and seven is in the middle." He checked the color chart taped beside his notebook. Cup D, if the chart was right, was a stronger base than cup B. That meant something invisible was different in the two cups, and the paper was the only way he could see it.

"The paper's doing all the work," Eden said, squinting at a strip like it was under a lens. "Where does it even come from? Nobody makes paper that just knows things."

A woman stopped at the booth, an older woman with a canvas bag, and looked at the strips. "That's litmus," she said. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens."

"Lichens?" Oakley said.

"The crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark. The grey patches, like the ones all over my garden wall."

Mason set down his tongs. He had been scraping grey crust off the north side of his grandmother's stone wall just last weekend, thinking it was some kind of dirt. It had a name, and it was hiding in the little strips on his table. He could hardly believe something off a rock could turn pink in lemon juice.

He worked through cups E and F. E turned the paper only a pale pink, a weak acid. F turned it a deep red, a strong one, low on the scale. He lined up all six strips in order beside the cups, and the pattern showed itself, weakest to strongest, like a row of sunset colors.

Ms. Mansour came by with her clipboard. "Verdict?"

"Acid, base, base, strong base, weak acid, strong acid," Mason said. He pointed at the strips. "And I know what the paper is. Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens. The crusty growths on rocks and tree bark."

"Where did you learn that?" she asked, raising an eyebrow.

"A visitor told me." He had been sure all morning that the paper was some kind of plastic invention, and now he was sure he was wrong, and both of those things felt strange and good at once. "Ms. Mansour, after the fair, could I bring some liquid from home and test it? I want to know what my grandma's well water is."

"Bring a sample Monday," she said, and moved on to the next booth.

Mason picked up the deepest red strip and held it up to the gymnasium lights.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In French, "Excusez-moi" is used to get a stranger's attention politely before asking a question, and "s'il vous plaît" means please.
story:
Lillian had been staring at the same French worksheet for twenty minutes when she finally raised her hand. "Mr. Sow, if I ask someone for directions in Paris, how do I even get them to stop and listen to me first?"

Mr. Sow smiled but didn't answer. "Listen to the recording from Tuesday again," he said. "The answer is in there." That was typical. He liked to make them hunt for things.

At the table by the window, Masen slid his headphones toward her. "It's the one where the woman asks where the post office is," he said. "Imogen swears she memorized it, but she says the first part sounds like two different words and she can't tell them apart."

Lillian put the headphones on. The woman on the recording began with "Excusez-moi," then asked her question, then ended with "s'il vous plaît." On the second listen, Lillian noticed something the others had missed. The "Excusez-moi" came before the question, every time, and the other word came at the end, like a tag. She rewound it three times. Was one of them just "please"? And if so, what was the other one for?

She tried a test on Imogen, who had lived in Montreal until she was seven. "Pretend you're on a street and I need directions," Lillian said. Then she jumped straight into her question without saying anything first. Imogen blinked at her, startled, and said it felt rude, like being ambushed. "You have to get my attention first," Imogen said. "In French you'd say 'Excusez-moi' before you ask anything. It's how you politely stop a stranger." Then Lillian added "s'il vous plaît" at the end of her second attempt, and Imogen nodded. "See? That one means please."

So the two words had different jobs, and the order mattered. Lillian wrote it on the back of her worksheet with a little arrow diagram, converting the whole recording into three steps: stop the person, ask, be polite. It reminded her of the mock election her civics class had run last month, where you had to sign in, mark your ballot, then hand it over in exactly that sequence. Skip a step and the whole thing fell apart.

On Friday, Mr. Sow set up a game. The classroom became a pretend city with taped streets on the floor, and everyone had to give and follow directions in French while a fan blew papers off the desks in a turbulent rush whenever someone "missed the train." Masen got lost twice, but Lillian walked straight to the paper bakery, stopped her stranger with "Excusez-moi," asked her question, and finished with "s'il vous plaît."

Mr. Sow checked his stopwatch. "Three minutes and nobody had to rescue you," he said. "Where is the bakery, again?"

"A droite, après la banque," said Lillian, pointing at the tape.

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: A small amount of stress before a test or a game can sharpen focus; stress becomes harmful mainly when it lasts for a long time without relief.
story:
The waiting room smelled like mint and something like new crayons, and Victoria kept her hands folded so nobody would see them shaking. She had chipped a corner off a back molar in her sleep, and the dentist, Ms. Virtanen, had asked one question that stuck in her head all morning: "Any chance you've been grinding your teeth at night?" Victoria hadn't known that was a thing a person could do without waking up. It made her wonder what else her body was doing while she wasn't paying attention.

"Open wide," Ms. Virtanen said, her mask fogging slightly. The little mirror clicked against Victoria's teeth like a spoon against a cup. "There it is. Your jaw muscles are tight as wire. That usually means something's been going on for a while, not just one bad night."

Victoria thought about that while the drill whined somewhere far from her mouth, numbed and distant. The swim meet was in nine days, and she'd been jittery about it for weeks, since Coach pinned the roster to the bulletin board. Her stomach hurt at breakfast. She'd stopped reading before bed and just lay in the dark instead, jaw clenched, rehearsing the flip turn over and over. She remembered Freyja at practice on Tuesday, sitting on the gutter with her goggles off, saying quietly, "I've felt awful for weeks. Not nervous-awful. Just awful." Victoria had told her the jitters were normal. Now she wasn't sure that answer had been coherent, or even kind.

Back at school, she found Freyja at the lunch table and slid her tray down beside her. "I need to tell you what I figured out," Victoria said. "Remember how I said the jitters are normal? I think I was only half right. A small amount of stress before a race actually sharpens you. It's stress that lasts for weeks without letting up that hurts you. Mine's been going on so long I cracked a tooth in my sleep." She touched her cheek where the filling was. "So I'm testing something. Four counts in, six counts out, ten times, every night, and lights out at nine-thirty instead of lying there rehearsing. If the jaw loosens up, I'll know it was the stress and not just bad luck."

Freyja turned her juice carton slowly in her hands, like it might symbolize something neither of them could name yet. "Weeks without letting up," she repeated. "That's me."

"Then you should talk to someone," Victoria said. "Not me. The counselor, or your mom. I felt guilty all through lunch for brushing you off on Tuesday, and I'm not doing it again."

"You didn't brush me off. You just didn't know yet."

"Come with me after school?" Victoria asked. "I'll walk you to the counseling office. You can bring the juice."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: A split is the time for one section of a race; an 800-metre runner's 400-metre split shows right away whether the first lap was faster or slower than planned.
story:
Sawyer had lost the same race twice, and both times the same thing had happened: a strong first lap, then legs that felt like wet sand on the second. He had decided the problem was that he wasn't trying hard enough. Quincy, who was timing him in the backyard with a stopwatch and a stopwatch only, had decided the problem was Sawyer.

"Sixty-two seconds!" Quincy shouted as Sawyer pounded past the fence post for the first lap of the third practice race. Sawyer raised a hand to show he'd heard, and kept sprinting. At the halfway point of lap two, his legs made an abrupt decision without him, slowing to a shuffle while Quincy jogged alongside, tapping the watch. "You died. Again. Same place as Tuesday."

Sawyer bent over, hands on knees, breathing like a leaky tire. Sixty-two seconds. He'd wanted to go out fast, because fast was obviously better, and twice now fast had turned into a walk by the end. But Quincy's number gave him a strange idea. If the watch showed exactly how fast the first lap had been, then he could tell, right away, whether the lap was faster or slower than planned. He didn't have to guess from how his lungs felt. "Time me again," he said. "And yell the number at the fence post. It's called a split, right? The time for one section."

"A what?"

"A split. My dad says it at meets."

Quincy, who wanted nothing more than to be the kind of person with an official job at a race, straightened up and held the stopwatch like a clipboard. "Fine. Official splitter." Sawyer set off again, and this time, when Quincy bellowed "Sixty-two!" at the post, Sawyer deliberately eased back. "Seventy!" came the shout on the next one, which was too slow, and Sawyer nudged the pace up. Around the final turn his legs still complained, but they carried him across the line at something like a run.

Sawyer walked a slow circle in the grass, doing the math out loud. Sixty-six per lap would be a lot better than one at sixty-two and one at a crawl. He couldn't see the pace itself, but the split made it visible, like footprints in snow. He had been wrong about needing more effort, and it was annoying how long he'd justified sprinting the first lap just because it felt good at the moment. Speed at the start came at the expense of speed at the end, and the watch had finally proven it.

"One more," Sawyer said, lining up at the fence.

Quincy raised the stopwatch. "Official splitter standing by."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Laundry is sorted by colour because new dark or bright clothes can release dye into the wash water, and that dye can tint white and pale clothes.
story:
The washer hummed like a hive, and Hudson stood in front of it with his mom's instructions scrawled on a receipt: sort, cold water, half a cap of soap. His mom was on nights at the hospital all week, and the basket at home had finally become a mountain, so here he was at Sud City Laundromat on a Saturday morning with nine dollars in quarters and no idea what "sort" actually meant.

"Toss it all in one load," said Tomas, who had tagged along because his own mom said he couldn't sit around the house all weekend. Tomas's family washed everything together, whites and darks and everything between, and he was already loading a lump of mixed clothes into the machine next to Hudson's. "Saves money."

Hudson looked at his own basket. There were his white school shirts, folded flat on top, and underneath them the new red gym socks he'd only worn twice. He dumped everything out onto the folding table and started making piles anyway, because something about the receipt's first word nagged at him. Whites here, darks there, reds in their own small stack. Was that right? He wondered why it would matter. Water was water.

Ms. Rao, who ran the flower shop next door and did her laundry here every Saturday, glanced over from the machine by the window. "Now that's a coherent system," she said, nodding at his piles. "Lights, darks, brights. Most people just shove it all in." She went back to her magazine, and Hudson felt weirdly proud of three lumps of dirty clothes.

He ran the whites first, then the brights, and while the machines churned, Tomas told him about getting his flu vaccine on Monday, which he was dreading. "My arm's going to be sore for two days," Tomas said. "Coach says we don't cease practice for anything, so I'll be doing push-ups with a dead arm."

When Tomas's load finished, he yanked it out and held up a T-shirt that had been white three days ago. It was pale pink now, splotchy across the chest. "What?" Tomas said, turning it around. "How did this happen?"

Hudson peered into Tomas's drum. At the very back, balled up and dripping, was a single new red sock. He remembered his own three stacks, and a question formed in his mind, the kind you could actually test. "Your red sock," he said. "It's new, right? Never been washed much?" Tomas shrugged. Hudson laid the pink shirt on the table next to a still-white one from his own brights load. "Mine went in with the reds, alone. Yours went in with everything. The red sock did something to the water, and the water did something to your shirt." He didn't know exactly how, but the pattern was right there on the table: same sock, different loads, different shirts.

Tomas held the pink shirt up to the light and groaned. "My mom's going to think I tie-dyed it on purpose." He started refolding it, as if pressing hard enough might squeeze the pink back out. Hudson pulled his last load from the dryer while it was still warm, shook out a white school shirt, and folded it along the seams the way his mom did, collar flat, sleeves back. It was white. It smelled like clean. He stacked it on top of the brights and the darks, all of it folded, all of it sorted, and he thought maybe next Saturday he'd try hot water on the towels, just to see.

"Hey," Tomas said, still staring at his ruined shirt. "Next time, show me those piles."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
James sat at the computer after dinner, scrolling through baseball stats while his dad washed dishes behind him. He had one goal tonight: prove to Aicha that his favorite player, Marino, was better than her favorite, Ellison. She had laughed at him at lunch and said the numbers settled it, because Ellison's batting average was thirty points higher. James wanted to find something that unsettled it.

He pulled up the season page for both players. Marino was hitting .262, and Ellison was at .294. His stomach dropped a little. Then he noticed the column next to it, the one labeled walks, and Marino's number was huge, way bigger than Ellison's. Why did that matter? He clicked into the fine print at the bottom of the page, the part most people never read, and found the definition. A batting average was hits divided by official at-bats, and walks did not count as at-bats at all.

He leaned closer to the screen. So a batter got no credit for walks. None. Marino had gotten on base over and over without it showing up anywhere in that famous number. James opened a spreadsheet and typed in the numbers himself: hits, at-bats, walks, plate appearances. He did the division twice because he didn't trust himself. When he counted times on base against total times up, Marino was actually ahead of Ellison. It felt like finding a hidden room in a house he'd lived in his whole life.

He snapped a screenshot and texted Aicha. "Marino got on base more often than Ellison. Look." Then he added, "The batting average leaves out all his walks."

Her reply came fast. "That's not a real stat, you drafted that out of nowhere."

"Draft this," he typed, and pasted the numbers. Then, because she would absolutely check, he added the fine print about at-bats so she could see it herself. His dad drifted over, drying a pan, and squinted at the screen. "That's a lot of columns," he said. James explained only the conclusion, not the arithmetic, and his dad nodded slowly. "So the number everybody quotes is kind of predatory, in a way. It hunts the parts that look good and swallows the rest." James laughed at that. He hadn't thought of a stat as something with teeth before.

Aicha's next message took three minutes, which meant she was calculating. "Okay. Fine. But his jersey is still ugly."

"Your whole argument is hormones and ugly jerseys?" he wrote back. He was joking, mostly, but he was also still thinking. If one number could hide something this big, what else was compressed like that? News headlines did it too, he realized, turning a whole season, a whole year, a whole city into a single ranking. He wondered how many invisible walks were hidden inside every number people threw around.

He opened a new tab and started a list: batting average, on-base percentage, everything he could find. At the top he typed one question in bold. "What did this number leave out?"

His dad looked over his shoulder and said, "You're going to be at that computer all night, aren't you."

"Probably," said James.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
story:
Zoey had measured the gym floor with a tape measure eleven times, and the ball still refused to cooperate. Her project, "How Fast Does a Ball Really Roll?", needed one clean run: a marble released at the top of a ramp, then timed at one-metre intervals across the smooth floor. At the science fair table, the stopwatch in Toby's hand, she watched the second hand of her whole plan start to wobble.

"Toby, you're flinching before I say go," she said. "That's why your times keep coming out too small."

"I'm not flinching. I'm nervous." Toby set the stopwatch down and straightened his own display, the one about which battery brand lasted longest. He wanted the physics prize more than he had admitted to anyone, and Zoey knew it, because last week in the cafeteria he had shown her the prize ribbon from the year before, frayed at the corner, and said his older brother had won it twice. "If I mess up your timing, I'll never forgive myself."

She remembered then the afternoon her grandmother had taught her to bake bread, kneading the dough in even strokes while saying, "The same push, every time, that's the whole secret." Zoey had thought that was just about bread. Now she wondered whether a ball worked the same way, and whether her graph would prove it.

They tried again. Toby pressed start when she called, and they wrote the numbers together on a napkin: one metre at two seconds, two metres at four, three metres at six. Zoey plotted the points on her graph paper, drew the line through them, and stared. It was straight, and it climbed at one unbroken slant from corner to corner, as if a ruler had been laid along the dots. She checked for a mistake, recalculated, and checked again. "It's straight," she said. "A straight sloping line means constant speed." The ball had rolled at exactly the same speed the whole way, steady as her grandmother's hands on the dough, and the graph had caught it in the act.

Mr. Wright stopped at their table, badge lanyard swinging, and leaned over the paper. "Walk me through it," he said, so Zoey did, pointing at each point: distance along the bottom, time up the side, the slope unbroken. When she finished, he nodded slowly. "Consistent data," he said. "That's rarer than you'd think." Then he noticed Toby hovering and added, "And your battery chart. Fair warning, the judges like a percentage breakdown of results."

"I have one," Toby said. "Sixty-three versus fifty-eight." He flourished the chart out from behind the poster board before he could lose his nerve.

"Then let's go find you a judge," Zoey said, and grabbed his sleeve.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: A word problem can be turned into an equation: if a taxi charges 3 dollars plus 2 dollars per kilometre and a ride costs 15, then 3 + 2k = 15, so k = 6.
story:
Sydney sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with a taxi receipt flattened in front of her like evidence. "Grandma, it says fifteen dollars. Didn't you say the hotel was four kilometres away?"

Her grandmother peeled carrots at the counter. "The driver said six, but he didn't take the pretty route. I never argue with a man holding my luggage."

Sydney frowned at the receipt. Somewhere in those numbers was the truth about how far they had actually driven, and she wanted to find it. On the back of an envelope she wrote what she knew: three dollars just to get in the taxi, then two dollars for every kilometre. She remembered the driver saying it at the curb, and there it was in small print at the bottom of the receipt too.

"So three plus two times the kilometres equals fifteen," she said slowly, and wrote 3 + 2k = 15. "If I could get the k alone, I'd know the distance."

She remembered Ms. Pritchard saying that an equation was like a balance, and that whatever you did to one side you had to do to the other. Sydney took away three from one side, so she took away three from the other. That left 2k = 12. Two k's made twelve, so one k had to be six. She sat back. Six kilometres. The driver had told the truth, and Grandma had doubted him all weekend.

She checked it a different way, because a good result deserved a second test. Three plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two, plus two. Fifteen. It wasn't a trivial little coincidence either, she decided; it was a rule, and rules meant you could use them again.

"I can infer the route from the money," she announced. "You went six kilometres, not four. Maybe there was a detour, or maybe this receipt is an anomaly and you got a discount you didn't notice."

Her grandmother set down the knife. "A what?"

"Something that doesn't fit the pattern. But it fits here. Six kilometres, fifteen dollars, exactly."

Griffin would not believe this when Sydney texted him. He had told her just last week that math had nothing to do with real life. She took a photo of the envelope and sent it with the message, "Grandma's taxi ride, solved." Then she turned the envelope over and wrote a new question at the top: what if the ride had cost twenty-three dollars?

Her grandmother slid a peeled carrot across the table. "You do the next one," she said, "and I'll check the driver's stories."
